subject: math
title: Data and Statistics: Center, Spread, Graphs, Probability, and Counting
objectives: You will find the mean, median, mode, and range of a data set, including data in a frequency table, and explain how an outlier affects the mean and the median.
You will use totals to find a missing value when the mean is known and to compute weighted averages and combined means.
You will read and interpret bar graphs, line graphs, circle graphs, and tables to find values, differences, and percents.
You will find the probability of simple events, complements, and compound events, with and without replacement.
You will count outcomes with the fundamental counting principle and tell when order matters (permutations) and when it does not (combinations).

slides.title: Week 4 Math: Data and Statistics
slides.board:
Data and Statistics

Center, Spread, Graphs, Probability, and Counting

  • Find the mean, median, mode, and range; spot an outlier
  • Use totals: missing values and weighted averages
  • Read bar, line, and circle graphs and tables
  • Find simple and compound probabilities
  • Count outcomes; tell permutations from combinations

Today: warm-up, center and spread, totals and averages, graphs, probability, counting, GED-style questions

notes.say: Welcome to Week 4. Today is about data: the numbers on a pay stub, a grocery receipt, a news graph, or a medical report. Data questions show up on the GED math test, and the same graph-reading skills show up again on the Science and Social Studies tests, so today pays off three times. You may use a calculator for most of this, but I still want every setup written on paper, because the setup is where the points are won or lost.
ask: When you hear "the average price of a house," what do you think that number means? (expected answer: any; listen for "add them up and divide" and come back to it on the outlier slide)
notes.watch: Pacing for 60 minutes: warm-up 5 min (slide 2); center and spread 12 min (slides 3–8); totals and averages 12 min (slides 9–14); graphs 9 min (slides 15–18); probability 10 min (slides 19–23); counting 7 min (slides 24–26); strategy and recap 5 min (slides 27–28). If you fall behind, cut the we-do slides to two problems each.

slides.title: Warm-up: Week 3 Review
slides.board:
Last week: exponents, roots, and scientific notation. No calculator.

  1. 25
  2. √81 + 32
  3. −42
  4. Write 0.00052 in scientific notation.
  5. (3 × 104)(2 × 103)
steps: 3. The exponent applies only to 4: −(4 × 4) = −16. Compare (−4)2 = 16.
4. Move the decimal point 4 places right to get 5.2. A small number gets a negative exponent: 5.2 × 10−4
5. Multiply the front numbers and add the exponents: 3 × 2 = 6 and 4 + 3 = 7, so 6 × 107

notes.say: Let's wake up last week's skills before we start something new. Take about three minutes and work all five on paper. Number 3 is the one to slow down on: read exactly what the exponent is attached to. When you are done, read me your answers one at a time and I will reveal each one.
ask: What did you get for number 3, and why? (expected answer: −16, because the exponent belongs to the 4 only and the negative sign is applied after)
In number 5, why do we add the exponents? (expected answer: multiplying powers of the same base adds the exponents: 10<sup>4</sup> × 10<sup>3</sup> = 10<sup>7</sup>)
notes.watch: An answer of 10 on number 1 means the student multiplied base by exponent; write out the five 2s. An answer of 16 on number 3 means the negative was squared; ask "Is there a parentheses around −4?" On number 4, 5.2 × 10<sup>4</sup> means the student used a positive exponent for a small number.

slides.title: Center and Spread
slides.board:
MeasureWhat it tells youHow to find it
MeanThe averageAdd all values; divide by how many values
MedianThe middleSort first. Odd count: the middle value. Even count: average the two middle values
ModeThe most commonThe value that appears most often (can be none, or more than one)
RangeThe spreadGreatest − least

notes.say: A data set is just a list of numbers about one thing, like your weekly hours or your last six electric bills. We describe it two ways: what is a typical value, which we call the center, and how spread out the numbers are. Mean, median, and mode are three different ways to describe the center. Range describes the spread. The most important habit today: before you find a median, rewrite the list in order.
ask: A list has 9 values. Which position is the median, once the list is sorted? (expected answer: the 5th; four values on each side)
A list has 10 values. Which positions do you average? (expected answer: the 5th and 6th)
notes.watch: Students often divide by the number of different values. If a value repeats, it still counts every time. Have the student count the values out loud before dividing.

slides.title: Four Measures from One Data Set
slides.board:
Rosa's weekly grocery bills for six weeks:

$72, $95, $88, $95, $110, $80

Find the mean, median, mode, and range.
steps: Median: sort first: 72, 80, 88, 95, 95, 110. Six values, so average the 3rd and 4th: (88 + 95) ÷ 2 = 183 ÷ 2 = $91.50
Mode: 95 appears twice; every other value appears once: $95
Notice: the three centers ($90, $91.50, $95) are close but not equal. A GED question may list all of them as choices.

notes.say: Watch how I organize this: one line per measure, and I sort the list once and reuse it. With an even number of values there is no single middle value, so the median is halfway between the two middle ones. That is why the median here, $91.50, is not even one of Rosa's bills, and that is fine.
ask: If I took the middle of the list as written, which two numbers would I average? (expected answer: 88 and 95, the 3rd and 4th as written; here that happens to give the same answer by luck, so always sort anyway)
notes.watch: If the student says the median is 88 or 95, they picked one middle value. With six values there are two middle values; average them.

slides.title: Outliers and Frequency Tables
slides.board:
An outlier is a value far from the rest. It pulls the mean toward it but barely moves the median.

DataMeanMedian
30, 32, 35, 38, 403535
30, 32, 35, 38, 1405535

Frequency table: each value is listed once with how many times it occurs. Total count = sum of the frequencies. Total of the data = sum of (value × frequency).

notes.say: Look at the two rows. I changed only one number, 40 to 140. The median did not move at all, but the mean jumped from 35 to 55, and 55 is bigger than four of the five values. That is why news reports about home prices and incomes use the median: a few very large values would make the mean misleading. Next, frequency tables. They are a shortcut for long lists. If the table says the value 2 has a frequency of 7, that means 2 appears seven times in the list.
ask: Which measure would you use to describe a typical salary at a company where the owner earns ten times what everyone else earns? Why? (expected answer: the median, because the owner's salary is an outlier that pulls the mean up)
notes.watch: In frequency tables, students often average the values in the left column and ignore the frequencies. Ask: "How many people are in this table?" The answer is the sum of the frequency column, not the number of rows.

slides.title: Median and Mean from a Frequency Table
slides.board:
A survey asked 20 households how many children live there.

Children01234
Households46721

Find the mean, median, and mode.
steps: Median: 20 values, so average the 10th and 11th. The 0s fill positions 1–4, the 1s fill 5–10, and the 2s fill 11–17. 10th = 1 and 11th = 2, so the median is (1 + 2) ÷ 2 = 1.5
Mode: the value with the greatest frequency is 2 (7 households).
Trap check: averaging only the left column, (0 + 1 + 2 + 3 + 4) ÷ 5 = 2, ignores how many households have each value.

notes.say: The table stands for a list of 20 numbers: four 0s, six 1s, seven 2s, two 3s, and one 4. For the mean, multiply each value by its frequency to get the total. For the median, count positions with a running total until you reach the middle. You never have to write out all 20 numbers.
ask: Which positions are the middle ones with 20 values? (expected answer: the 10th and 11th)
What is the mode: 2 or 7? (expected answer: 2; 7 is how many times it occurs)
notes.watch: A student who says the mode is 7 read the frequency instead of the value. A student who divides 30 by 5 used the number of columns instead of the number of households.

slides.title: Center and Spread Together
slides.board:
1. Find the mean, median, mode, and range of 5, 12, 7, 12, 9.
  2. Add an outlier, 55, to that list. Find the new mean and median. Which one changed more?
  3. Find the median of 4, 11, 6, 9.
steps: 1. Sum: 5 + 12 + 7 + 12 + 9 = 45; mean = 45 ÷ 5 = 9. Sorted: 5, 7, 9, 12, 12, so median = 9. Mode = 12. Range = 12 − 5 = 7.
2. New sum: 45 + 55 = 100, and now there are 6 values: 100 ÷ 6 ≈ 16.7. Sorted: 5, 7, 9, 12, 12, 55, so median = (9 + 12) ÷ 2 = 10.5. The mean rose by about 7.7; the median rose by only 1.5.

notes.say: Let's do these together. Before each one, tell me your first move. For number 2, do not start over: you already know the old sum, so just add 55 to it, and remember the count goes up by one.
ask: In number 2, what do we divide by now? (expected answer: 6, because there are six values)
In number 3, what are the two middle values after sorting? (expected answer: 6 and 9)
notes.answer: (1) mean 9, median 9, mode 12, range 7   (2) mean ≈ 16.7, median 10.5; the mean changed much more   (3) 7.5
notes.watch: On number 2, a mean of 20 means the student divided 100 by 5 and forgot the new value increases the count. On number 3, 8.5 means they averaged 6 and 11, the middle of the unsorted list.

slides.title: Your Turn: Center and Spread
slides.board:
Three minutes. Work on paper, then tell me your answers.

  1. Find the mean of 18, 25, 30, 27.
  2. Find the median of 13, 7, 22, 9, 16, 30.
  3. Find the mode and the range of 4, 8, 4, 9, 2, 8, 4.

notes.say: Your turn. I am starting a three-minute clock. Write which measure you are finding at the top of each problem before you compute; that habit is your protection against the GED's favorite trap. When time is up, read me your answers.
ask: Read me your answers. (expected answer: 25; 14.5; mode 4 and range 7)
notes.answer: (1) 18 + 25 + 30 + 27 = 100; 100 ÷ 4 = 25   (2) sorted: 7, 9, 13, 16, 22, 30; (13 + 16) ÷ 2 = 14.5   (3) 4 appears three times, so the mode is 4; range = 9 − 2 = 7
notes.watch: On number 2, an answer of 15.5 means the student averaged 22 and 9, the 3rd and 4th values as written; send them back to sort. On number 3, a mode of 8 means they stopped counting after 8 appeared twice; 4 appears three times.

slides.title: Use the Total: Missing Values and Weighted Averages
slides.board:
mean × number of values = total

Missing value: total needed − total you have.

Combined groups: add the group totals, then divide by the total number of people.

Weighted average: multiply each value by its weight, add, then divide by the total weight. If the weights are percents that add to 100%, just add the products.

notes.say: Every problem on this slide is solved the same way: go through the total. If the mean of 5 tests is 80, the 5 tests add up to 400. That one fact lets you find a missing score, combine two classes, or figure out a grade where some parts count more than others. When values do not all count equally, you need a weighted average, and the plain average of the numbers will be wrong.
ask: The mean of 4 numbers is 15. What is their total? (expected answer: 60)
Tests count 60% and homework counts 40%. Do they count equally? (expected answer: no; tests count more, so use a weighted average)
notes.watch: The most common wrong move is averaging averages: (78 + 88) ÷ 2 for two classes of different sizes. Ask: "Do both groups have the same number of people?" If not, go through the totals.

slides.title: Find the Missing Score
slides.board:
Keisha's first four test scores are 88, 74, 91, and 79.

What score does she need on the fifth test so that the mean of all five tests is 85?

notes.say: Three lines: the total I need, the total I have, and the difference. Notice I multiplied by 5, not 4, because the goal is a mean of all five tests. Then I check by putting 93 back into the list. On the GED, 85 itself will usually be one of the choices, as a trap for people who answer with the target mean.
ask: Why multiply 85 by 5 and not by 4? (expected answer: the mean of 85 is for all five tests)
notes.watch: A student who answers 8 multiplied 85 by 4 (340 − 332). A student who answers 85 gave the target mean. Ask them to check their answer by computing the new mean.

slides.title: Weighted Average: A Course Grade
slides.board:
PartWeightScore
Homework25%92
Quizzes35%78
Final exam40%84

What is the course grade?
steps: Grade: 23 + 27.3 + 33.6 = 83.9 (the weights add to 100%, so no division is needed)
Compare: the simple average (92 + 78 + 84) ÷ 3 ≈ 84.7 is wrong, because it treats homework as if it counted as much as the final.

notes.say: Change each percent to a decimal, multiply it by its score, and add. Because the weights add to 100 percent, the sum is already the grade. Notice the grade is lower than the simple average: the high homework score counts for only a quarter of the grade.
ask: Which part of the grade has the most influence? (expected answer: the final exam, at 40%)
notes.watch: Students who add the three scores and divide by 3 are using a simple average. Students who forget to change 25% to 0.25 will get 2,300 for the first line; ask whether a grade can be over 100.

slides.title: Averages Together
slides.board:
1. The mean of six numbers is 15. Five of them are 12, 18, 9, 20, and 14. What is the sixth number?
  2. Class A has 15 students with a mean score of 82. Class B has 25 students with a mean score of 74. What is the mean score of all 40 students?
  3. The mean of five numbers is 20. One number is removed, and the mean of the other four is 18. What number was removed?
steps: 2. Class A total: 15 × 82 = 1,230. Class B total: 25 × 74 = 1,850. Combined: 3,080 ÷ 40 = 77. (Not 78, the simple average, because Class B is larger.)

notes.say: All three of these are total problems in disguise. For each one, tell me what total you will find first. Number 2 is the one most people miss: the answer is closer to 74 than to 82 because more students are in Class B.
ask: In number 2, should the combined mean be closer to 82 or to 74? Why? (expected answer: closer to 74, because Class B has more students)
In number 3, what are the two totals? (expected answer: 100 before and 72 after)
notes.watch: On number 2, an answer of 78 is the simple average of 82 and 74. On number 3, an answer of 2 is the difference of the means, not of the totals.

slides.title: GED-Style Question: Missing Value
slides.board:
Marisol's first five paychecks this year had a mean of $640. What must her sixth paycheck be so that the mean of all six paychecks is $660?

A. $660    B. $680    C. $760    D. $3,960
steps: Eliminate A ($660): that is the target mean, not the paycheck needed. A sixth check of $660 cannot raise the mean from $640 all the way to $660.
Eliminate B ($680): it comes from thinking "the mean goes up $20, so the check is $20 more than $660." The new check must lift all six paychecks by $20 each.
Eliminate D ($3,960): that is the total needed for six paychecks (660 × 6), not the sixth paycheck. Stopping one step early.
C ($760) is correct: total needed 660 × 6 = 3,960; total so far 640 × 5 = 3,200; 3,960 − 3,200 = $760.

notes.say: Here we do not even know the five paychecks, only their mean. That is fine: the mean times the count gives the total. Work it first, then use the choices as a checklist of traps. Each wrong choice is an answer someone gets by a real mistake.
ask: What is the total of the first five paychecks? (expected answer: $3,200)
Which choice did you get? (expected answer: C, $760)
notes.watch: If the student chose D, they found the total and stopped. Have them reread the question and underline "sixth paycheck."

slides.title: Your Turn: Totals and Averages
slides.board:
Four minutes. A calculator is fine.

  1. Quiz scores: 70, 82, 75, 88. What score on the fifth quiz gives a mean of 80?
  2. A store mixes 20 pounds of beans that cost $3 per pound with 30 pounds that cost $5 per pound. What is the cost per pound of the mix?
  3. Tests count 60% and homework counts 40%. Test average 72; homework average 95. What is the grade?

notes.say: Your turn. For each problem, write the total first. On number 2, ask yourself whether the answer should be closer to $3 or to $5 before you calculate.
ask: Read me your three answers. (expected answer: 85; $4.20; 81.2)
notes.watch: On number 2, $4.00 is the simple average of $3 and $5; more of the mix is the $5 beans, so the answer must be above $4. On number 3, 83.5 is the simple average of 72 and 95.

slides.title: Reading Graphs and Tables
slides.board:
Before any question, read: title → axis labels → units → scale (what one gridline is worth).

DisplayBest forKey move
Bar graphComparing categoriesRead straight across from the top of the bar
Line graphChange over timeSteepest upward segment = greatest increase
Circle graphParts of a wholeAmount = percent × total; angle = percent × 360°
TableExact valuesFind the row and column; check the units

notes.say: Most wrong answers on graph questions are not math mistakes. They are reading mistakes: the wrong bar, the wrong unit, or assuming each gridline is worth 1 when it is worth 5 or 20. So before you answer, say the title, the units, and the scale out loud. On a line graph, an increase means the line goes up from left to right; a big drop is a big change, but it is not an increase. On a circle graph, the percents add to 100%, so a missing section is 100% minus the rest.
ask: A bar graph's axis says "Sales (thousands of dollars)." A bar reaches 45. What were the sales? (expected answer: $45,000)
On a circle graph, what angle is a 25% section? (expected answer: 90°)
notes.watch: Watch for students who answer "greatest change" questions with a decrease when the question asks for an increase. Have them say "up" or "down" for each segment first.

slides.title: Reading a Line Graph
slides.board:
A line graph shows a shop's monthly sales (in units). The plotted points are:

JanFebMarAprMayJun
120135128160155190

(a) Between which two months was the greatest increase? (b) What was the percent increase from March to April?
steps: Changes: Jan–Feb +15; Feb–Mar −7; Mar–Apr +32; Apr–May −5; May–Jun +35.
(a) The largest increase is +35: May to June. (Mar–Apr, +32, is close, so compute; do not eyeball.)
(b) Percent change = change ÷ original. Change: 160 − 128 = 32. Original (March): 128.

notes.say: First I list every month-to-month change with its sign. Then the question is easy to answer, and I can see the trap: March to April looks steep, but May to June is a little bigger. For the percent increase, divide by the starting value, the earlier month. That is last week's percent change rule, from Week 2, coming back.
ask: For the percent increase, do we divide by 128 or by 160? Why? (expected answer: 128, the original, earlier value)
notes.watch: A student who gets 20% divided by 160, the new value. A student who picks March to April eyeballed the graph instead of computing each change.

slides.title: Reading a Circle Graph
slides.board:
A circle graph shows how a family spends its $3,600 monthly income:

RentFoodTransportationUtilitiesOtherSavings
35%18%12%9%16%?

(a) What percent is savings? (b) How many dollars is that? (c) How many degrees is the food section?
steps: (a) The sections add to 100%: 35 + 18 + 12 + 9 + 16 = 90, so savings = 100% − 90% = 10%

notes.say: A circle graph is one whole, and the percents always add to 100. That lets you find a missing section. Then any section's dollar amount is its percent times the total, and its angle is its percent times 360 degrees, because a full circle is 360 degrees.
ask: How many degrees would a 50% section be? (expected answer: 180°)
notes.watch: Students sometimes answer (b) with 10, the percent. Ask: "The question asks how many dollars. Does 10 have a dollar sign?"

slides.board:
A survey asked 200 adults how they prefer to shop.

  1. What percent of all the adults prefer online shopping?
  2. What percent of the adults 40 and over prefer shopping in a store?
  3. One adult is chosen at random. What is the probability that the person is under 40 and prefers shopping in a store?

notes.say: This kind of table, with rows and columns that both mean something, is called a two-way table. The key question every time is: "Out of whom?" That tells you which total goes on the bottom of your fraction. Notice that number 3 is a probability question. Tables are a common way the GED asks about probability, which is our next topic.
ask: In number 2, what goes on the bottom of the fraction? (expected answer: 100, the number of adults 40 and over)
notes.watch: On number 2, 27.5% means the student divided 55 by 200 (everyone) instead of by the 100 people in that row. Ask "Out of whom?"

slides.title: Probability Basics
slides.board:
P(event) = favorable outcomes ÷ total outcomes (all outcomes equally likely)

  • Always from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain). Write it as a fraction, decimal, or percent.
  • Complement: P(not A) = 1 − P(A)
  • "Or" with no overlap: count all the favorable outcomes together
  • Predict: expected number = probability × number of tries

notes.say: Probability is a fraction: what you want over everything that could happen. A number cube has six equally likely outcomes, so the chance of rolling a 5 is 1 out of 6. If something is impossible the probability is 0; if it is certain, 1. A probability can never be bigger than 1, so if you get 1.3, you made a mistake. The complement rule saves time: the chance something does not happen is 1 minus the chance it does.
ask: A number cube is rolled. What is P(even)? (expected answer: 3/6 = 1/2)
If P(rain) = 0.3, what is P(no rain)? (expected answer: 0.7)
A spinner lands on blue 18 times in 60 spins. About how many blues would you expect in 200 spins? (expected answer: 18/60 = 0.3, and 0.3 × 200 = 60)
notes.watch: Students often write favorable to unfavorable (3 blue to 9 others is 3/9) instead of favorable to total (3/12). Always put the total on the bottom.

slides.title: Compound Events: "And" Means Multiply
slides.board:
For P(A and B), multiply: P(A) × P(second event, after the first one happens).

TypeExampleSecond probability
Independentcoin and cube; drawing with replacementDoes not change
Dependentdrawing without replacementTotal goes down by 1; favorable may too

P(heads and 6) = 1/2 × 1/6 = 1/12

notes.say: When two things must both happen, multiply. A combined event is always less likely than either part, which is why the answer gets smaller. The only question is whether the first event changes the second. If you put the item back, or the events have nothing to do with each other, nothing changes. If you keep the first item, there is one fewer item for the second draw, so the total goes down by one, and if the first item was the kind you wanted, the favorable count goes down too.
ask: A bag has 3 red and 2 blue chips. You draw a red chip and keep it. How many chips are left, and how many are red? (expected answer: 4 chips left; 2 red)
notes.watch: Two errors to listen for: adding the probabilities for "and," and using the same fraction twice when the problem says "without replacement." If a student adds, point out that 1/2 + 1/6 = 2/3 would make "heads and 6" more likely than rolling a 6 alone.

slides.title: One Bag, Four Questions
slides.board:
A bag holds 4 red, 6 blue, and 2 green marbles (12 in all).

  1. P(green)
  2. P(not red)
  3. Draw two with replacement: P(red, then red)
  4. Draw two without replacement: P(red, then red)
steps: (b) P(red) = 4/12 = 1/3, so P(not red) = 1 − 1/3 = 2/3 (or count: 8 non-red out of 12)
(c) Put it back, so nothing changes: 4/12 × 4/12 = 1/3 × 1/3 = 1/9
(d) Keep the first red marble: 3 red remain out of 11. 4/12 × 3/11 = 12/132 = 1/11
Notice (d) is smaller than (c): taking a red marble out makes a second red less likely.

notes.say: One bag, four kinds of questions. For each draw, I ask two things: how many are there in all right now, and how many of those do I want? With replacement, those numbers reset. Without replacement, I update both before the second draw.
ask: In part (d), why is it 3/11 and not 4/12 for the second draw? (expected answer: one red marble was removed, so 3 red remain out of 11)
notes.watch: If the student gets 1/9 for part (d), they ignored "without replacement." If they get 3/12 for the second draw, they reduced the red count but not the total.

slides.title: Probability Together
slides.board:
1. A number cube is rolled. What is P(a number less than 3)?
  2. A coin is flipped and a number cube is rolled. What is P(tails and a 5 or 6)?
  3. A box holds 10 light bulbs; 3 are defective. Two are chosen without replacement. What is P(both work)?
  4. A spinner landed on blue 18 times in 60 spins. Predict the number of blues in 200 spins.
steps: 3. 7 work. First: 7/10. Then 6 working out of 9: 6/9. 7/10 × 6/9 = 42/90 = 7/15

notes.say: Let's do these together. For each one, tell me first whether it is a single event, an "and" with independent events, or an "and" without replacement. Number 3 asks about the bulbs that work, so count those first.
ask: In number 3, how many bulbs work? (expected answer: 7)
In number 4, what is the experimental probability of blue? (expected answer: 18/60 = 0.3)
notes.watch: On number 3, 3/10 × 2/9 = 1/15 means the student found P(both defective). Ask them to reread what the question wants.

slides.title: GED-Style Question: Without Replacement
slides.board:
A cooler holds 7 apple juice boxes and 5 orange juice boxes. Lee takes two boxes at random, one after the other, without putting the first one back. What is the probability that both boxes are orange juice?

A. 5/12    B. 25/144    C. 5/33    D. 9/23
steps: Eliminate A (5/12): that is only the first draw. "Both" means two events, so multiply by the second probability.
Eliminate B (25/144): it comes from 5/12 × 5/12, as if the first box were put back. Without replacement, 4 orange boxes remain out of 11.
Eliminate D (9/23): it comes from adding tops and bottoms, (5 + 4)/(12 + 11). Probabilities of "and" events are multiplied, not added.

notes.say: Read the question twice and underline "without putting the first one back." That phrase changes the second fraction. Work it, then use the wrong answers as a list of the mistakes you avoided.
ask: After Lee takes one orange box, how many boxes are left, and how many are orange? (expected answer: 11 left; 4 orange)
notes.watch: If the student chose B, have them act it out with 12 slips of paper: take one away and count what is left.

slides.title: Counting: Multiply the Choices
slides.board:
Counting principle: if you make several choices in a row, multiply the number of options for each.

QuestionOrder matters?MethodExample (from 5 people)
Fill different roles or placesYes: permutationMultiply downPresident, VP: 5 × 4 = 20
Choose a groupNo: combinationOrdered count ÷ arrangements of the groupPick 2 for a team: 20 ÷ 2 = 10

Test: if you swap two people, is it a different result?

notes.say: Three shirts and four pairs of pants make twelve outfits, not seven: for each shirt you have four choices of pants. That is the counting principle. When you choose people one at a time without repeats, the number of options goes down by one each time. Then ask the swap question. If Ana as president and Ben as vice president is different from Ben as president and Ana as vice president, order matters. If you are just picking two people for a team, Ana-and-Ben is the same team as Ben-and-Ana, so you divide out the repeats.
ask: How many ways can 3 people line up for a photo? (expected answer: 3 × 2 × 1 = 6)
Choosing 3 people from a group: by what number do we divide the ordered count? (expected answer: 6, the number of ways to arrange 3 people)
notes.watch: Students often add the options (3 + 4 = 7). Have them list the outfits for one shirt first; they will see four outfits per shirt.

slides.title: Three Counting Questions
slides.board:
1. A lock uses a 3-digit code, digits 0–9. How many codes if digits can repeat? If they cannot repeat?
  2. Five books are lined up on a shelf. How many orders are possible?
  3. A committee of 3 is chosen from 8 volunteers. How many committees are possible?
steps: (b) 5 × 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 = 120 (order matters: it is a different shelf)
(c) Ordered: 8 × 7 × 6 = 336. Each group of 3 can be arranged 3 × 2 × 1 = 6 ways, all the same committee.

notes.say: For each question I ask: how many choices for the first spot, the second, the third? And can I reuse a choice? Then the swap test. A lock code of 1-2-3 is not the same as 3-2-1, so order matters. A committee of Ana, Ben, and Cy is the same committee no matter who was picked first, so divide out the 6 orders.
ask: In (c), why divide by 6? (expected answer: three people can be arranged 3 × 2 × 1 = 6 ways, and all six are the same committee)
notes.watch: In (c), 336 means the student forgot to divide. In (a), 30 means they added 10 + 10 + 10 instead of multiplying.

slides.title: Your Turn: Probability and Counting
slides.board:
Three minutes.

  1. A number cube is rolled. What is P(not a 6)?
  2. A uniform has 4 shirts, 3 pants, and 2 shoe styles. How many uniforms?
  3. A club of 9 chooses a president and a vice president. How many ways?
  4. The same club chooses 2 members to attend a meeting. How many ways?

notes.say: Last solo round. For numbers 3 and 4, write "order matters" or "order does not matter" next to each before you compute. I am starting the clock.
ask: Read me your four answers. (expected answer: 5/6; 24; 72; 36)
notes.answer: (1) 1 − 1/6 = 5/6   (2) 4 × 3 × 2 = 24   (3) different roles, order matters: 9 × 8 = 72   (4) a pair, order does not matter: 72 ÷ 2 = 36
notes.watch: If numbers 3 and 4 come back with the same answer, the student did not apply the swap test. If number 2 comes back as 9, they added.

slides.title: GED Strategy: Name It, Then Use the Choices
slides.board:
1. Name the measure. Underline mean, median, mode, range, or "probability of both."
  2. Write the setup on your note board: the total, the sorted list, or the fractions.
  3. Use the calculator for the arithmetic (Part 2). Enter a fraction with the n/d key.
  4. Sense check: Is the mean between the least and greatest value? Is the probability between 0 and 1? Is "and" smaller than each part?

The formula sheet defines the mean and median only. Know the rest by heart.

notes.say: GED data questions love to list the mean, median, mode, and range of the same data as the four choices, so every choice looks like a real number. Your protection is to name the measure before you compute and check that the number you choose answers that word. The calculator handles the arithmetic, but it cannot sort a list or decide whether order matters; that is your job. And remember, the formula sheet gives the mean and median only. Probability, counting, mode, range, and weighted averages you must know cold.
ask: A GED question asks for the median, and the choices include the mean. How do you protect yourself? (expected answer: underline "median," sort the list, and check that the chosen number is the middle value)
notes.watch: Students who rush often skip sorting because the calculator feels like it "did the work." Ask them to say which measure the question asks for before they touch the calculator.

slides.title: Recap and What Comes Next
slides.board:
• Mean = sum ÷ count. Median: sort, then find the middle. Mode: most often. Range: greatest − least. Outliers pull the mean, not the median.
  • Use the total: mean × count = total. Weighted average: multiply each value by its weight, add, divide by the total weight.
  • Graphs: title, labels, units, scale. Circle graph amount = percent × total.
  • Probability = favorable ÷ total. "And" means multiply; without replacement, update the counts.
  • Counting: multiply the choices. Order matters: permutation. Order does not matter: divide out the repeats.

screens.title: What You Will Learn
screens.html:
This lesson is about data: lists of numbers, graphs, tables, and chances. These skills appear on the GED math test, and the graph and table skills come back on the Science and Social Studies tests too. Work through one screen at a time. Most screens teach one idea, show a worked example, and end with a quick check you answer before moving on.

By the end, you will be able to:

  • Find the mean, median, mode, and range of a data set, including one given in a frequency table, and explain how an outlier affects them.
  • Use totals to find a missing value and to compute a weighted average.
  • Read bar graphs, line graphs, circle graphs, and tables.
  • Find the probability of simple events and of compound events, with and without replacement.
  • Count outcomes, and tell when order matters (permutations) and when it does not (combinations).

You may use a calculator for this lesson, but write every setup on paper first.

screens.title: The Mean
screens.html:
The mean is what most people call the average. To find it:

  1. Add all the values.
  2. Count how many values there are, including repeats.
  3. Divide the sum by the count.

The mean is always somewhere between the smallest and the largest value. If your answer is outside that range, check your work.

example.prompt: Seven workers' commute times, in minutes, are 25, 40, 30, 25, 35, 45, and 52. Find the mean.

check.prompt: A food truck sold 46, 52, 38, 61, and 48 tacos on five days. What is the mean number of tacos sold per day?

mistakes.why: You divided by 4. There are five days, so divide the total by 5: 245 ÷ 5 = 49.
That is the total. The mean is the total divided by the number of days: 245 ÷ 5 = 49.
That is the range (61 − 38), which measures spread. The mean is the sum divided by the count.

check.hint: Add the five numbers, then divide by how many numbers there are.
check.explain:
Sum: 46 + 52 + 38 + 61 + 48 = 245.

Count: 5 days.

Mean: 245 ÷ 5 = 49 tacos.

Check: 49 is between the least value (38) and the greatest (61).

screens.title: The Median
screens.html:
The median is the middle value. Always sort the list first, from least to greatest.

  • Odd number of values: the median is the one in the middle. With 7 values, it is the 4th.
  • Even number of values: there are two middle values. The median is their mean: add them and divide by 2.

The median of an unsorted list is not the middle number as written. Sort first, every time.

steps: Six values, so the middle two are the 3rd and 4th: 12 and 14.

check.prompt: The ages of six people in a training class are 34, 29, 41, 25, 38, and 30. What is the median age?

mistakes.why: You averaged 41 and 25, the middle two numbers of the list as written. Sort first: 25, 29, 30, 34, 38, 41. The middle two are 30 and 34.
With six values there are two middle values, 30 and 34. The median is halfway between them: (30 + 34) ÷ 2 = 32.
You added the two middle values but did not divide by 2: 64 ÷ 2 = 32.

check.hint: Put the ages in order. With six values, which two are in the middle?
check.explain:
Sort: 25, 29, 30, 34, 38, 41.

Six values, so the middle two are the 3rd and 4th: 30 and 34.

Median: (30 + 34) ÷ 2 = 32.

If you got 33, you used the middle of the unsorted list (41 and 25).

screens.title: Mode and Range
screens.html:
The mode is the value that appears most often. A data set can have one mode, more than one mode, or no mode at all (when no value repeats).

The range is the greatest value minus the least value. It does not describe a typical value; it tells you how spread out the data are. A small range means the values are close together.

You do not have to sort to find the range, but sorting makes it easy to spot the greatest and least values without missing one.

example.prompt: Find the mode and range of 6, 3, 8, 3, 10, 6, 3.
steps: Count each value: 3 appears three times, 6 appears twice, 8 and 10 appear once.

check.prompt: A pharmacy filled 14, 7, 22, 7, 5, and 18 prescriptions per hour over six hours. What is the range of these numbers?

mistakes.why: You subtracted the first value from the last value as listed (18 − 14). The range uses the greatest value (22) and the least value (5).
That is the mode, the value that appears most often. The range is greatest minus least: 22 − 5 = 17.
You added the greatest and least values. The range is their difference: 22 − 5 = 17.

check.hint: Find the greatest value and the least value. Then subtract.
check.explain:
Greatest value: 22. Least value: 5.

Range: 22 − 5 = 17.

If you got 4, you used the first and last numbers in the list instead of the greatest and least.

screens.title: Outliers: Mean or Median?
screens.html:
An outlier is a value much greater or much less than the rest of the data. An outlier pulls the mean toward it, but it barely moves the median, because the median depends only on the middle position.

Example: the salaries 30, 32, 35, 38, 40 (in thousands) have a mean and median of 35. Change 40 to 140. The median is still 35, but the mean jumps to 55, which is higher than four of the five salaries.

When a data set has an outlier, the median usually describes a typical value better. That is why reports on home prices and household incomes use the median.

check.prompt: The monthly rents in a small building are $850, $900, $875, $925, and $2,400. Which measure best describes a typical rent in the building?
options: The median, $900, because the $2,400 rent pulls the mean above most rents
The mean, $1,190, because it is the only measure that uses every rent
The range, $1,550, because it shows how much the highest rent costs
The median, $875, because it is the middle rent in the list as given
why: The mean is $1,190 (5,950 ÷ 5), but four of the five rents are under $930. The $2,400 outlier pulls the mean up, so it does not describe a typical rent.
The range ($2,400 − $850 = $1,550) measures spread, not a typical value. It also is not the cost of the highest rent.
$875 is the middle of the list as written. Sorted, the rents are 850, 875, 900, 925, 2,400, so the median is $900.
check.hint: Is there a value far from the others? Which measure does that value pull?
check.explain:
Mean: (850 + 900 + 875 + 925 + 2,400) ÷ 5 = 5,950 ÷ 5 = $1,190.

Sorted: 850, 875, 900, 925, 2,400, so the median is $900.

$2,400 is an outlier. It pulls the mean up to $1,190, which is more than four of the five rents. The median, $900, describes a typical rent better.

The tempting wrong answer is the $875 median: that is the middle of the unsorted list.

screens.title: Frequency Tables
screens.html:
A frequency table lists each value once, along with how many times it occurs (its frequency). A dot plot shows the same information with stacked dots.

  • Count of values = sum of the frequencies.
  • Total of the data = sum of (value × frequency).
  • Mean = total ÷ count.
  • Median: keep a running count of the frequencies to find the middle position.
  • Mode = the value with the greatest frequency (not the frequency itself).

example.prompt: Ten people reported how many cups of coffee they drink per day: 0 cups (1 person), 1 cup (2 people), 2 cups (4 people), 3 cups (2 people), 4 cups (1 person). Find the mean and the median.
steps: Median: the 5th and 6th values. Position 1 is 0; positions 2–3 are 1; positions 4–7 are 2. Both middle values are 2, so the median is 2.

check.prompt:
The table shows the number of days 20 students were absent last month.

Days absent01235
Number of students58421

What is the mean number of days absent?

mistakes.why: You averaged the five values in the top row, (0 + 1 + 2 + 3 + 5) ÷ 5. Each value must be counted as many times as its frequency.
You divided the total, 27, by 5, the number of columns. Divide by the number of students: 27 ÷ 20 = 1.35.
That is the total number of days absent. Divide by the 20 students to get the mean.

check.hint: Multiply each number of days by its number of students and add. Then divide by the total number of students.
check.explain:
Total days: 0(5) + 1(8) + 2(4) + 3(2) + 5(1) = 0 + 8 + 8 + 6 + 5 = 27.

Students: 5 + 8 + 4 + 2 + 1 = 20.

Mean: 27 ÷ 20 = 1.35 days.

A common mistake is to average 0, 1, 2, 3, and 5 (which gives 2.2), ignoring how many students had each value.

screens.title: Finding a Missing Value
screens.html:
Turn the mean formula around: mean × number of values = total. Then:

  1. Multiply the target mean by the number of values to get the total you need.
  2. Add the values you already have.
  3. Subtract. The difference is the missing value.

Check by putting your answer back in and finding the mean.

example.prompt: Ana bowled 132, 148, 155, and 141 in four games. What must she score in the fifth game to have a mean of 145 for all five games?

check.prompt: Tyrell's electric bills for five months were $96, $104, $88, $112, and $95. What must his sixth bill be so that the mean of all six bills is $100?

mistakes.why: $100 is the target mean, not the bill needed. Go through the total: 100 × 6 = 600, and 600 − 495 = 105.
You multiplied 100 by 5. The mean is for all six bills, so the total needed is 100 × 6 = 600.
That is the mean of the first five bills (495 ÷ 5). Find the total needed for six bills and subtract what he has.

check.hint: What total do six bills need to have a mean of $100?

screens.title: Combining Groups
screens.html:
When two groups have different sizes, you cannot just average their means. Go through the totals:

  1. Find each group's total: mean × number in the group.
  2. Add the totals.
  3. Divide by the total number of items or people.

The combined mean is always closer to the mean of the larger group. This is a weighted average: each group counts in proportion to its size.

example.prompt: Kim worked 30 hours at $16 per hour and 10 hours at $24 per hour. What was her average pay per hour?
steps: 720 ÷ 40 = $18 per hour (closer to $16, where she worked more hours).

check.prompt: A company has 8 day-shift workers who earn a mean of $17 per hour and 12 night-shift workers who earn a mean of $21 per hour. What is the mean hourly pay of all 20 workers?

mistakes.why: That is the simple average of $17 and $21. There are more night-shift workers, so the mean is pulled toward $21.
That is the total hourly pay of all 20 workers. Divide by 20 to get the mean.
You divided the total, 388, by 10. There are 8 + 12 = 20 workers, so divide by 20.

check.hint: Find the total hourly pay for each shift, add them, and divide by the total number of workers.
check.explain:
Day shift total: 8 × 17 = 136.

Night shift total: 12 × 21 = 252.

All workers: (136 + 252) ÷ 20 = 388 ÷ 20 = $19.40.

The simple average, $19, is wrong because the two groups are different sizes.

screens.title: Weighted Averages with Percents
screens.html:
Course grades often give each part a percent weight. When the weights add to 100%, the method is short:

  1. Change each percent to a decimal.
  2. Multiply each score by its decimal weight.
  3. Add the products. That sum is the weighted average.

The part with the biggest weight has the biggest effect on the result.

example.prompt: Quizzes count 40% and tests count 60%. Jamal's quiz average is 90 and his test average is 75. What is his grade?
example.answer: 81 (the simple average, 82.5, would overrate the quizzes)

check.prompt: In a course, homework counts 20%, quizzes count 30%, and the final exam counts 50%. Maya's homework average is 90, her quiz average is 76, and her final exam score is 84. What is her course grade?

mistakes.why: That is the simple average of 90, 76, and 84. The final exam counts much more than homework, so multiply each score by its weight first.
That is the sum of the three scores. Multiply each score by its weight and add the products.
You added the weighted products and then multiplied by 3. When the weights add to 100%, the sum of the products is the grade.

check.hint: Change each percent to a decimal and multiply it by its score. Then add.
check.explain:
Homework: 0.20 × 90 = 18.

Quizzes: 0.30 × 76 = 22.8.

Final: 0.50 × 84 = 42.

Grade: 18 + 22.8 + 42 = 82.8.

The simple average, about 83.3, is wrong because it counts homework as much as the final.

screens.title: Bar Graphs and Line Graphs
screens.html:
Before you answer a graph question, read four things: the title, the axis labels, the units, and the scale (what each gridline is worth).

  • Bar graphs compare categories. Read straight across from the top of the bar to the scale.
  • Line graphs show change over time. An upward segment is an increase; a downward segment is a decrease. The steepest upward segment is the greatest increase.

To compare two points, find each value, then subtract. Write the values down instead of eyeballing.

check.prompt: The line graph shows the number of people enrolled in a free evening class each week. What was the greatest increase in enrollment from one week to the next?

mistakes.why: That is the rise from the lowest point (40) to the highest point (90), across several weeks. The question asks for the greatest change from one week to the next.
That is the increase from Week 1 to Week 2 (or Week 4 to Week 5). The increase from Week 3 to Week 4 is larger: 75 − 50 = 25.
That is the greatest enrollment, not the greatest increase. Subtract each week from the next week.

check.hint: Write down each week's value. Then find each week-to-week change.
check.explain:
Values: 40, 55, 50, 75, 90, 85.

Changes: +15, −5, +25, +15, −5.

The greatest increase is from Week 3 to Week 4: 75 − 50 = 25 people.

50 is the overall rise from the lowest to the highest point, which spans more than one week.

screens.title: Circle Graphs
screens.html:
A circle graph (pie chart) shows parts of one whole. The sections are usually labeled with percents, and the percents add to 100%.

  • Amount in a section = percent × total.
  • Missing section = 100% − the other sections.
  • Angle of a section = percent × 360°.
  • To combine sections, add their percents first, then multiply by the total.

example.prompt: A circle graph shows the favorite sports of 200 people. The football section is 45%. How many people chose football? How many degrees is that section?

check.prompt: A circle graph shows how 640 workers get to work: car 55%, bus 15%, bicycle 10%, walking 20%. How many more workers drive a car than walk?

mistakes.why: That is the difference in percents. Multiply the percent by the number of workers: 0.35 × 640 = 224.
That is the number who drive a car (0.55 × 640). Subtract the number who walk (128).
That is the number who walk. The question asks how many more drive than walk.

check.hint: Find the difference in percents, then multiply by the total number of workers.

screens.title: Tables and Two-Way Tables
screens.html:
In a table, find the right row and column first, then read the cell. Check the units in the title or headings (for example, "in thousands").

A two-way table sorts the same people by two categories, one in the rows and one in the columns. For a percent or a fraction, always ask: "Out of whom?" That group's total goes on the bottom.

  • Out of everyone: divide by the grand total.
  • Out of one row or one column: divide by that row's or column's total.

check.prompt:
The table shows the plans of 200 gym members.

Monthly planAnnual planTotal
Under 30483280
30 and over3684120
Total84116200

What percent of all the members have an annual plan?

mistakes.why: That is the number of members with an annual plan. Divide by the 200 members to get a percent: 116 ÷ 200 = 58%.
You used only the members 30 and over (84 ÷ 120). The question asks about all the members.
You used only the members under 30 (32 ÷ 80). The question asks about all the members.

check.hint: Out of whom? Find the total for the annual plan column and divide by the grand total.

screens.title: Probability Basics
screens.html:
Probability tells how likely an event is: P = favorable outcomes ÷ total outcomes, when all outcomes are equally likely.

  • A probability is from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain). It can be a fraction, decimal, or percent.
  • Complement: the chance something does not happen is P(not A) = 1 − P(A).
  • Prediction: expected number = probability × number of tries. If a spinner lands on blue 18 times in 60 spins, expect about 0.3 × 200 = 60 blues in 200 spins.

Put the total on the bottom, not the number of unfavorable outcomes.

example.prompt: A number cube (1 to 6) is rolled. Find P(greater than 4) and P(not greater than 4).
steps: Greater than 4: the outcomes 5 and 6. P = 2/6 = 1/3.

check.prompt:
A raffle sells 250 tickets, and one winning ticket is drawn. Dana buys 10 tickets. What is the probability that Dana does not win?

Enter a fraction or a decimal.

mistakes.why: That is the probability that Dana wins. The probability that she does not win is 1 − 1/25 = 24/25.
You compared Dana's tickets to the other tickets. Probability compares favorable outcomes to all 250 tickets.
That is the number of tickets that are not Dana's. Divide by the total number of tickets: 240/250.

check.hint: Find how many tickets are not Dana's. Put that over the total number of tickets.
check.explain:
Tickets that are not Dana's: 250 − 10 = 240.

P(not win) = 240/250 = 24/25 = 0.96.

Or use the complement: P(win) = 10/250 = 1/25, so P(not win) = 1 − 1/25 = 24/25.

screens.title: Independent Events: "And" Means Multiply
screens.html:
Two events are independent when one does not change the chances of the other: a coin and a number cube, two spins of a spinner, or two draws with replacement.

To find P(A and B), multiply: P(A) × P(B).

Sense check: "both" is always less likely than either one alone, so the product is smaller than each fraction. If you added and got a bigger number, you used the wrong operation.

example.prompt: Ten cards are numbered 1 to 10. You draw one, put it back, and draw again. What is the probability that both cards show a multiple of 3?
steps: With replacement, the draws are independent: 3/10 × 3/10 = 9/100.

check.prompt:
A spinner has 5 equal sections numbered 1 to 5. You spin it once and flip a coin. What is the probability of spinning an even number and getting heads?

Enter a fraction or a decimal.

mistakes.why: You added 2/5 and 1/2. For "and," multiply: 2/5 × 1/2 = 1/5.
That is the probability of an even number only. You also need heads, so multiply by 1/2.
You added the tops and the bottoms, (2 + 1)/(5 + 2). Multiply the probabilities instead: 2/5 × 1/2.

check.hint: Find P(even) on the spinner and P(heads) on the coin. "And" means multiply.
check.explain:
Even numbers on the spinner: 2 and 4, so P(even) = 2/5.

P(heads) = 1/2.

Independent, so multiply: 2/5 × 1/2 = 2/10 = 1/5.

screens.title: Dependent Events: Without Replacement
screens.html:
When you draw without replacement, the first draw changes the second. Before the second draw, update the counts:

  • The total goes down by 1.
  • If the first item was the kind you want, the favorable count also goes down by 1.

Then multiply as usual.

example.prompt: A bag has 3 red and 2 blue chips. Two are drawn without replacement. What is P(both red)?
steps: First draw: 3 red out of 5, so 3/5.
One red chip is gone: 2 red out of 4, so 2/4.

check.prompt: A jar holds 9 lime candies and 3 cherry candies. Lena takes one candy at random and eats it, then takes a second candy at random. What is the probability that both candies are cherry?
why: You used 3/12 for both draws, as if the first candy went back in the jar. After one cherry candy is eaten, 2 cherry remain out of 11.
You added the tops and the bottoms, (3 + 2)/(12 + 11). For "both," multiply the two probabilities.
That is the probability for the first candy only (3/12). "Both" means you must also multiply by the second probability, 2/11.
check.hint: Lena eats the first candy, so it does not go back. How many cherry candies and how many candies in all are left?
check.explain:
First candy: 3 cherry out of 12, so 3/12.

Second candy: 2 cherry out of 11, so 2/11.

3/12 × 2/11 = 6/132 = 1/22.

1/16 is the answer if the first candy were put back (3/12 × 3/12).

screens.title: The Counting Principle
screens.html:
If you make several choices in a row, multiply the number of options for each choice. This is the fundamental counting principle.

Example: 3 sizes and 5 flavors give 3 × 5 = 15 different drinks. For each size there are 5 flavors.

  • If choices can repeat (like digits in a code), each spot has the full number of options.
  • If choices cannot repeat, each spot has one fewer option than the last: 5 × 4 × 3 …

example.prompt: A diner offers 3 soups, 5 main dishes, and 4 desserts. How many meals of one soup, one main dish, and one dessert are possible?
steps: Three choices in a row, so multiply.

check.prompt: A car comes in 5 colors, 3 trim levels, and 2 engine types. How many different cars can be ordered with one color, one trim level, and one engine type?

mistakes.why: You added 5 + 3 + 2. For each color there are 3 trims, and for each of those there are 2 engines, so multiply.
You left out the engine choice. Multiply all three: 5 × 3 × 2 = 30.

check.hint: Each choice multiplies the number of possibilities.
check.explain:
5 colors × 3 trims × 2 engines = 30 cars.

Adding (5 + 3 + 2 = 10) undercounts: each color can go with every trim and every engine.

screens.title: Permutations and Combinations
screens.html:
Ask the swap test: if you swap two of the people or items, do you get a different result?

  • Yes: order matters (permutation). Roles, places, and arrangements. 1st, 2nd, and 3rd from 7 runners: 7 × 6 × 5 = 210.
  • No: order does not matter (combination). Groups, teams, and committees. Find the ordered count, then divide by the number of ways to arrange the group. A group of 3 can be arranged 3 × 2 × 1 = 6 ways, so 3 runners for a relay team from 7: 210 ÷ 6 = 35.

example.prompt: Choose 2 of 4 pizza toppings. How many pairs are possible?
steps: Each pair was counted twice (pepper-onion and onion-pepper), so divide by 2.

check.prompt: A manager will choose 3 of 10 applicants to interview together in one group meeting. How many different groups of 3 are possible?

mistakes.why: That counts ordered choices (10 × 9 × 8). The group is the same no matter who is picked first, so divide by 3 × 2 × 1 = 6.
You multiplied 10 by 3. Count the ordered choices, 10 × 9 × 8, then divide out the repeats.
That allows the same person to be picked more than once (10 × 10 × 10). Each applicant can be picked only once.

check.hint: Does order matter for a group? Count the ordered choices, then divide by the number of ways to arrange 3 people.
check.explain:
Ordered choices: 10 × 9 × 8 = 720.

Each group of 3 can be arranged 3 × 2 × 1 = 6 ways, and they are all the same group.

Groups: 720 ÷ 6 = 120.

screens.title: Summary
screens.html:
• Mean: sum ÷ number of values. Median: sort, then take the middle (or average the two middle values). Mode: most frequent. Range: greatest − least.
  • An outlier pulls the mean toward it; the median barely moves.
  • Frequency table: count = sum of frequencies; total = sum of value × frequency.
  • Use the total: mean × count = total. Missing value = total needed − total you have.
  • Weighted average: multiply each value by its weight, add, and divide by the total weight (no division if the weights are percents that add to 100%).
  • Graphs: read the title, labels, units, and scale first. Circle graph amount = percent × total. In a two-way table, ask "Out of whom?"
  • Probability = favorable ÷ total, from 0 to 1. P(not A) = 1 − P(A). "And" means multiply. Without replacement, update the counts.
  • Counting: multiply the choices. Order matters: permutation. Order does not matter: divide out the repeated arrangements.

Next: Practice Set A. If you score under 80%, practice the same skills again with Set B. Then take the Exit Check.

items.prompt: Renee's scores on five math quizzes were 78, 85, 92, 70, and 85. What is the mean of her quiz scores?

Committee (order does not matter): start with the 210 ordered choices. Each group of 3 people can be arranged in 3 × 2 × 1 = 6 orders, and all 6 orders are the same committee.

210 ÷ 6 = 35 committees. True.

343 = 7 × 7 × 7 would allow one person to hold more than one office, which the problem does not allow. 210 committees forgets to divide out the repeated orders. 21 = 7 × 3 multiplies the number of members by the number of positions, which is not a counting rule.

mistakes.why: You divided 66 by 200, all the students. The question says "of the students who passed," so divide by the 120 who passed.
You divided 66 by 88, which is the percent of prep-class students who passed. The question asks what percent of the students who passed took a class.
That is the percent of all students who passed (120 ÷ 200). The question asks about the students who passed, and which of them took a class.

items.hint: "Of the students who passed" tells you which total goes on the bottom.
items.explain:
Students who passed: 120.

Of those, 66 took a prep class.

66 ÷ 120 = 0.55 = 55%.

75% (66 ÷ 88) answers a different question: what percent of the prep-class students passed.

items.prompt: The mean weight of 5 packages is 12 pounds. One package is removed, and the mean weight of the remaining 4 packages is 10.5 pounds. How many pounds did the removed package weigh?

mistakes.why: That is the change in the mean, not the weight of the package. Go through the totals: 5 × 12 = 60 and 4 × 10.5 = 42.
That is the total weight of the 4 remaining packages. Subtract it from the total of all 5: 60 − 42 = 18.
That is the total weight of all 5 packages. Subtract the weight of the 4 that remain: 60 − 42 = 18.

items.hint: Find the total weight before and after the package was removed.
items.explain:
Total of 5 packages: 12 × 5 = 60 pounds.

Total of 4 packages: 10.5 × 4 = 42 pounds.

Removed package: 60 − 42 = 18 pounds.

Sense check: removing a package heavier than 12 pounds should lower the mean, and it did.

items.prompt:
A driver recorded seven delivery times, in minutes:

32, 45, 28, 38, 45, 52, 40

Which statement is true?
options: The mean and the median are both 40 minutes.
The median is 38 minutes and the mode is 45 minutes.
The mean is 46.7 minutes and the range is 24 minutes.
The mode is 45 minutes and the range is 20 minutes.
why: The mode is 45, but 38 is the middle of the list as written. Sorted, the times are 28, 32, 38, 40, 45, 45, 52, so the median is 40.
The range is 24, but 46.7 comes from dividing the sum, 280, by 6. There are seven times, so the mean is 280 ÷ 7 = 40.
The mode is 45, but the range is not 20. You subtracted the first listed time (32) from the greatest; the least time is 28, so the range is 52 − 28 = 24.
items.explain:
Sum: 32 + 45 + 28 + 38 + 45 + 52 + 40 = 280; mean = 280 ÷ 7 = 40.

Sorted: 28, 32, 38, 40, 45, 45, 52; median = 40 (the 4th value).

Mode = 45; range = 52 − 28 = 24.

So the mean and the median are both 40 minutes. The tempting choice with a median of 38 uses the unsorted list.

items.prompt: Jalen's commissions for his first four weeks at a new job were $310, $285, $342, and $263. What must his commission be in the fifth week so that his mean weekly commission for the five weeks is $320?

mistakes.why: $320 is the target mean, not the commission needed. His first four weeks average only $300, so the fifth must be much higher.
You multiplied 320 by 4. The mean is for five weeks, so the total needed is 320 × 5 = 1,600.
That is the mean of his first four weeks (1,200 ÷ 4). Find the total needed for five weeks and subtract what he has.

items.explain:
Total needed: 320 × 5 = 1,600.

Total so far: 310 + 285 + 342 + 263 = 1,200.

Fifth week: 1,600 − 1,200 = $400.

Check: 1,600 ÷ 5 = 320.

items.prompt: In a course, tests count 45%, projects count 25%, and the final exam counts 30% of the grade. Andre's test average is 78, his project average is 92, and his final exam score is 85. What is his course grade?

mistakes.why: That is the simple average of 78, 92, and 85. Tests count much more than projects, so multiply each score by its weight first.
That is the sum of the three scores. Multiply each score by its weight and add the products.
You multiplied the weighted sum by 3. When the weights add to 100%, the sum of the products is the grade.

items.explain:
Tests: 0.45 × 78 = 35.1.

Projects: 0.25 × 92 = 23.

Final: 0.30 × 85 = 25.5.

Grade: 35.1 + 23 + 25.5 = 83.6.

The simple average, 85, is wrong because tests carry the most weight and his test average is his lowest score.

items.prompt:
The line graph shows the number of customers who entered a store during each hour from 9 a.m. to 3 p.m. Each point is labeled with the hour that the count began.

Between which two consecutive hours did the number of customers increase the most?
options: 11 a.m. to 12 p.m.
9 a.m. to 10 a.m.
1 p.m. to 2 p.m.
12 p.m. to 1 p.m.
why: The count rose from 20 to 35, an increase of 15. From 11 a.m. to 12 p.m. it rose from 30 to 60, an increase of 30.
The count fell from 55 to 20. That is the biggest change on the graph, but it is a decrease, not an increase.
These are the two highest points, but the count fell from 60 to 55 between them. The question asks for the greatest increase.
items.explain:
Values: 9 a.m. 20, 10 a.m. 35, 11 a.m. 30, 12 p.m. 60, 1 p.m. 55, 2 p.m. 20.

Changes: +15, −5, +30, −5, −35.

The greatest increase is +30, from 11 a.m. to 12 p.m.

1 p.m. to 2 p.m. has the largest change (35), but the line goes down there, so it is a decrease.

items.prompt: A circle graph shows how 1,500 survey respondents prefer to receive appointment reminders: email 28%, text message 46%, and phone call for the rest. How many respondents prefer a phone call?

mistakes.why: That is the percent who prefer a phone call. The question asks how many people: 0.26 × 1,500 = 390.
That is the number who prefer email or text (74% of 1,500). Phone calls are the remaining 26%.
That is the number who prefer text messages (0.46 × 1,500). Find the phone call percent first: 100% − 28% − 46% = 26%.

items.explain:
Phone call percent: 100% − 28% − 46% = 26%.

Respondents: 0.26 × 1,500 = 390.

Check: email 420 + text 690 + phone 390 = 1,500.

items.prompt: Fifteen raffle tickets are in a hat, and 6 of them belong to the Lee family. Two winning tickets are drawn at random, one after the other. The first ticket is not returned to the hat. What is the probability that both winning tickets belong to the Lee family?
why: You used 6/15 for both draws (6/15 × 6/15 = 36/225 = 4/25), as if the first ticket went back in the hat. After one Lee ticket is drawn, 5 Lee tickets remain out of 14.
You added the tops and the bottoms, (6 + 5)/(15 + 14). For "both," multiply: 6/15 × 5/14.
2/5 = 6/15 is the probability for the first draw only. "Both" means you must also multiply by the second probability, 5/14.
items.explain:
First draw: 6 Lee tickets out of 15, so 6/15.

Second draw: 5 Lee tickets out of 14, so 5/14.

6/15 × 5/14 = 30/210 = 1/7.

4/25 is the answer only if the first ticket were returned.

items.prompt:
A pizza shop offers 3 crusts, 2 sauces, and 7 toppings. Each pizza has 1 crust, 1 sauce, and exactly 2 different toppings.

Choose the option that makes each statement true.

The number of ways to choose 2 different toppings is {{0}}.

The number of different pizzas the shop can make is {{1}}.

why: You multiplied 7 by 2, the number of toppings chosen. Count ordered choices, 7 × 6 = 42, then divide by 2.
42 = 7 × 6 counts each pair twice (mushroom-olive and olive-mushroom are the same pizza). Divide by 2: 21.
49 = 7 × 7 allows the same topping twice. The toppings must be different, so use 7 × 6, then divide by 2.
You added the 21 topping pairs to the 6 crust-and-sauce combinations (3 × 2 = 6). Each of those 6 combinations goes with every topping pair, so multiply: 6 × 21 = 126.
That is 3 × 2 × 7, which counts pizzas with only one topping. Each pizza has a pair of toppings, and there are 21 pairs.
You used 42 ordered topping pairs instead of 21: 3 × 2 × 42 = 252. The order of the toppings does not matter.

items.explain:
Toppings: order does not matter. Ordered choices: 7 × 6 = 42. Each pair is counted twice, so 42 ÷ 2 = 21.

Pizzas: 3 crusts × 2 sauces × 21 topping pairs = 126.

252 forgets that a pair of toppings is the same in either order.

items.prompt:
Six part-time workers each worked 12, 15, 14, 16, 13, and 14 hours last week. A seventh worker, who worked 42 hours, is added to the data.

Select two statements that are true.
options: The mean increases from 14 hours to 18 hours.
The median stays at 14 hours.
The median increases from 14 hours to 18 hours.
The mean increases from 14 hours to 21 hours.
The range stays at 4 hours.
why: The median depends only on the middle position. Sorted with the new value: 12, 13, 14, 14, 15, 16, 42. The 4th value is still 14.
You divided the new total, 126, by 6. With seven workers, divide by 7: 126 ÷ 7 = 18.
The range uses the greatest and least values. With 42 added, the range becomes 42 − 12 = 30.
items.explain:
Before: 12 + 15 + 14 + 16 + 13 + 14 = 84; mean = 84 ÷ 6 = 14. Sorted: 12, 13, 14, 14, 15, 16; median = (14 + 14) ÷ 2 = 14. Range = 4.

After: 84 + 42 = 126; mean = 126 ÷ 7 = 18. Sorted: 12, 13, 14, 14, 15, 16, 42; median = 14. Range = 30.

The outlier pulled the mean up by 4 hours but did not move the median.

items.prompt:
Kara's cell phone bills for eight months were $54, $61, $48, $75, $61, $58, $70, and $53.

Which statement is true?
options: The mean is $60 and the median is $59.50.
The median is $68 and the mode is $61.
The mean is $68.57 and the range is $27.
The mode is $61 and the range is $22.
why: The mode is $61, but $68 is the average of 75 and 61, the middle two bills as listed. Sorted, the middle two are 58 and 61, so the median is $59.50.
The range is $27, but $68.57 comes from dividing the sum, 480, by 7. There are eight bills, so the mean is 480 ÷ 8 = $60.
The mode is $61, but the range is not $22. You subtracted the last listed bill ($53) from the greatest; the least bill is $48, so the range is 75 − 48 = $27.
items.explain:
Sum: 54 + 61 + 48 + 75 + 61 + 58 + 70 + 53 = 480; mean = 480 ÷ 8 = $60.

Sorted: 48, 53, 54, 58, 61, 61, 70, 75; median = (58 + 61) ÷ 2 = $59.50.

Mode = $61; range = 75 − 48 = $27.

So the mean is $60 and the median is $59.50. The choice with a median of $68 uses the unsorted list.

items.prompt: Over 5 nights, a hotel had a mean of 84 rooms booked per night. After the 6th night, the mean for all 6 nights was 86 rooms. How many rooms were booked on the 6th night?

mistakes.why: 86 is the new mean. A 6th night with exactly 86 rooms could not raise the mean from 84 to 86.
That is the change in the mean. Go through the totals: 86 × 6 = 516 and 84 × 5 = 420.
You found the extra rooms needed to raise all six nights by 2 (2 × 6 = 12) but forgot to add them to the old mean: 84 + 12 = 96.

items.explain:
Total for 5 nights: 84 × 5 = 420.

Total for 6 nights: 86 × 6 = 516.

6th night: 516 − 420 = 96 rooms.

Check: 516 ÷ 6 = 86.

items.prompt: A store sold 120 shirts at $15 each, 80 shirts at $22 each, and 50 shirts at $30 each. What was the mean price of all the shirts sold, in dollars?

mistakes.why: That is the simple average of $15, $22, and $30. Far more shirts sold at $15, so the mean price must be closer to $15.
That is the total amount collected. Divide by the number of shirts, 120 + 80 + 50 = 250.
You divided the total, $5,060, by 3, the number of prices. Divide by the number of shirts, 250.

items.explain:
$15 shirts: 120 × 15 = $1,800.

$22 shirts: 80 × 22 = $1,760.

$30 shirts: 50 × 30 = $1,500.

Total: $5,060 for 250 shirts. Mean: 5,060 ÷ 250 = $20.24.

The simple average, about $22.33, ignores how many shirts sold at each price.

Between which two consecutive months did the number of new cards decrease the most?

The number fell from 165 to 150, a decrease of 15. From March to April it fell from 150 to 110, a decrease of 40.

items.prompt: A crew of 9 volunteers includes 4 teenagers. Two volunteers are chosen at random, one after the other, to lead a project. The same person cannot be chosen twice. What is the probability that neither leader is a teenager?
why: You used 5/9 for both choices (5/9 × 5/9 = 25/81), as if the first person could be chosen again. After one adult is picked, 4 adults remain out of 8.
1/6 is the probability that both leaders are teenagers (4/9 × 3/8). The question asks for neither, so use the 5 adults.
You added the tops and the bottoms, (5 + 4)/(9 + 8). For "both are adults," multiply: 5/9 × 4/8.
items.explain:
Volunteers who are not teenagers: 9 − 4 = 5.

First leader: 5/9. Second leader (one adult already chosen): 4/8.

5/9 × 4/8 = 20/72 = 5/18.

25/81 would be the answer only if the same person could be chosen twice.

items.prompt:
A running club has 10 members.

Choose the option that makes each statement true.

The number of ways to choose 3 members to serve as equal co-captains is {{0}}.

The number of ways to choose 3 members to run the 1st, 2nd, and 3rd legs of a relay is {{1}}.

why: You multiplied 10 by 3. Count ordered choices, 10 × 9 × 8 = 720, then divide by the 6 ways to arrange 3 people.
720 counts each group of co-captains 6 times, once for each order. Co-captains have equal roles, so divide: 720 ÷ 6 = 120.
1,000 = 10 × 10 × 10 allows one member to be chosen more than once.
You multiplied 10 by 3. Each leg is filled by a different member: 10 × 9 × 8.
120 is the number of groups. Relay legs are different positions, so order matters and you do not divide by 6.
1,000 = 10 × 10 × 10 lets one member run more than one leg.

items.explain:
Relay legs (order matters): 10 × 9 × 8 = 720.

Co-captains (order does not matter): each group of 3 appears 3 × 2 × 1 = 6 times among the 720, so 720 ÷ 6 = 120.

Swap test: switching two runners changes who runs which leg, but switching two co-captains changes nothing.

items.prompt:
The ages of five people in a training class are 22, 25, 24, 27, and 22. A 60-year-old joins the class.

Select two statements that are true.
options: The mean age increases from 24 years to 30 years.
The mode stays at 22 years.
The median age increases from 24 years to 30 years.
The mean age increases from 24 years to 36 years.
The range stays at 5 years.
why: The median depends only on the middle positions. Sorted with the new age: 22, 22, 24, 25, 27, 60. The median is (24 + 25) ÷ 2 = 24.5, not 30.
You divided the new total, 180, by 5. With six people, divide by 6: 180 ÷ 6 = 30.
With 60 added, the greatest value changes, so the range becomes 60 − 22 = 38.
items.explain:
Before: 22 + 25 + 24 + 27 + 22 = 120; mean = 24. Sorted: 22, 22, 24, 25, 27; median 24; mode 22; range 5.

After: 120 + 60 = 180; mean = 180 ÷ 6 = 30. Sorted: 22, 22, 24, 25, 27, 60; median = 24.5; mode still 22; range 38.

The outlier moved the mean by 6 years but the median by only half a year.

vocab.def: The average: the sum of the values divided by the number of values.
The middle value when the data are in order; with an even count, the average of the two middle values.
The value that appears most often in a data set; there may be more than one mode or none.
The greatest value minus the least value; a measure of spread.
A value much greater or much less than the rest of the data.
vocab.example: In 20, 22, 21, 95, the value 95 is an outlier.

vocab.def: An average in which some values count more than others; multiply each value by its weight before adding.
A graph that uses connected points to show how a quantity changes over time.
vocab.example: Monthly rainfall plotted from January to June

vocab.def: A graph that shows parts of a whole as sections of a circle, usually labeled with percents that add to 100%.
vocab.example: 25% of a circle graph is a section of 90°.

vocab.def: A number from 0 to 1 that tells how likely an event is: favorable outcomes divided by total outcomes. The probability that an event does not happen is 1 minus the probability that it does.
A table that lists each value once along with how many times it occurs (its frequency).
vocab.example: Value 2 with frequency 7 means the number 2 appears seven times in the data.

vocab.def: Events where the result of one does not change the probability of the other.
vocab.example: Flipping a coin and rolling a number cube

vocab.def: Events where the result of one changes the probability of the other, such as drawing without replacement.
vocab.example: Drawing two cards from a deck without putting the first one back

vocab.def: If one choice has m options and another has n options, there are m × n ways to make both choices.
A selection where order does not matter.

notes:
Week 4 Study Sheet: Data, Statistics, Probability, and Counting

Center and Spread

MeasureHow to find it
MeanSum ÷ number of values
MedianSort first; middle value (even count: average the two middle values)
ModeMost frequent value (can be none or several)
RangeGreatest − least

Example: 2, 4, 4, 7, 13 → mean 30 ÷ 5 = 6, median 4, mode 4, range 11.

An outlier pulls the mean, not the median. Frequency table: count = sum of frequencies; total = sum of (value × frequency).

Use the Total

mean × count = total

Missing value: total needed − total you have. Want a mean of 80 on 4 quizzes; have 72, 85, 78: 320 − 235 = 85.

Combined groups: (15 × 82 + 25 × 74) ÷ 40 = 77, not 78.

Weighted average: multiply each value by its weight, add, divide by the total weight. Percent weights that add to 100%: just add. 0.4 × 90 + 0.6 × 75 = 81.

Graphs and Tables

  • Read the title, labels, units, and scale first.
  • Bar graph: compare categories.
  • Line graph: change over time; steepest upward segment = greatest increase.
  • Circle graph: amount = percent × total; missing section = 100% − the rest; angle = percent × 360°.
  • Two-way table: ask "Out of whom?" That total goes on the bottom.

Probability

  • P = favorable ÷ total, from 0 to 1.
  • P(not A) = 1 − P(A).
  • "And": multiply. With replacement: same fraction each draw.
  • Without replacement: total goes down by 1 (and favorable too, if one was drawn).
  • Prediction: probability × number of tries.

4 red of 12, two draws without replacement: 4/12 × 3/11 = 1/11.

Counting

SituationMethodExample
Several choices in a rowMultiply the options3 sizes × 5 flavors = 15
Order matters (permutation): roles, placesMultiply downPresident and VP from 7: 7 × 6 = 42
Order does not matter (combination): groupsOrdered count ÷ arrangements of the groupChoose 3 of 5: 60 ÷ 6 = 10

Top mistakes: finding the median without sorting; dividing by the wrong count; averaging averages of different-size groups; using a simple average when values have different weights; misreading the scale; calling a decrease an increase; adding probabilities for "and"; ignoring "without replacement"; adding choices instead of multiplying.
